memory_candidates.content: To verify a bash script that calls bare `curl` deterministically without a real network, install a PATH-shadowing stub named `curl` ahead of the real one on PATH, and dispatch canned responses by request host inside the stub, keyed off per-host env vars (e.g. CURL_STUB_<HOST>_CODE / CURL_STUB_<HOST>_BODY). Support a magic code value (e.g. `curl_fail`) that makes the stub exit non-zero with no output, to simulate a genuine transport failure distinct from a stubbed non-200 HTTP response -- callers need both failure modes exercised separately. To test one function from a larger script in isolation (rather than running the whole script as a subprocess), extract just that function's definition plus its dependencies via `sed -n '/^fn_start() {/,/^next_fn() {/p' script.sh | sed '$d'`, prepend any required global variable assignments the extracted code references at its own top level (not just inside function bodies), and source/run the result in a scratch script. Capture the invoked function's own return status explicitly (`fn; rc=$?; ...; exit $rc`) rather than trusting the wrapper script's own exit code, which reflects only its last statement.

When adding N parallel provider/backend branches that must share one dedup/normalization/ID-derivation contract, give each provider function an identical (query, budget) -> 0|1 signature: return 0 the instant a real, parseable answer arrives (even an empty one), return 1 only on genuine failure, and communicate failure detail (reason, http_code) via caller-visible non-local variables rather than a second return channel. The orchestrating loop then advances to the next provider only on that 1, breaking immediately on any 0 -- this is what correctly distinguishes 'this provider ran and found nothing' from 'this provider could not run', a distinction worth preserving explicitly rather than collapsing both into a single failure/empty-array signal.
